title: Entry Threat: when a scary announcement is not a credible future action
real_world_setup: A large firm says it will start a price war if a smaller rival enters. The entrant hears the threat before deciding whether to enter, but the price war would also hurt the large firm after entry has already happened.
first_principles_question: Is the threat a real constraint on entry, or is it an announcement that will stop being attractive once the future decision point arrives?
modeling_path: Start by drawing the timing. The entrant moves first, then the incumbent reacts. That makes this a tree, not only a payoff table. Solve the incumbent's later choice first, then use that continuation to decide what the entrant should believe at the start.
mathematical_spine: The spine is backward recursion plus mutual consistency. A continuation action must be best for the player who takes it at that later node, and the full prediction must survive those later checks.
worked_walkthrough: Suppose entry gives the incumbent payoff -1 if it fights and 2 if it accommodates. The later node selects accommodate. The entrant should not treat fight as the continuation merely because the incumbent said it earlier. If entry is profitable against accommodation, the threat does not block entry in the model.
where_simple_story_breaks: The simple story says a powerful firm can threaten anything. The model breaks that story by asking whether carrying out the threat would still be rational later.
what_to_check_in_transcript: Look for the course's movement from representation of games into backward induction and subgame perfection. The evidence should support timing, later incentives, and credibility, not just the word threat.
why_this_case_matters: This case matters because it separates power from commitment. In ordinary language, having the ability to hurt a rival is not the same as having a reason to hurt the rival after the rival has already moved. That distinction is the heart of many strategic problems: threats in business, bargaining, politics, and platform governance can sound strong while being weak at the future decision point.
transfer_lesson: When transferring the lesson, look for any claim where an early statement is supposed to change someone else's choice. Ask who moves later, what they will know later, and whether the threatened action still serves their own payoff then. If the later action is costly to the threatener and no commitment device changes that cost, the early statement should be treated as talk, not as a binding constraint.
failure_audit: The transfer can fail if the incumbent has reputation at stake, long-run deterrence value, legal obligations, contract terms, or technology that commits it to fight. Those additions can make fighting rational even when a one-shot tree says accommodate. A serious paper should say whether those forces are absent, small, or explicitly included in the continuation payoff before using the simple entry-deterrence lesson.

title: Tacit Cartel: when cooperation depends on the weight of the future
real_world_setup: Several sellers keep prices high without signing an explicit agreement. Each seller can earn more this week by secretly undercutting, but rivals may punish future cheating with lower prices.
first_principles_question: Can repeated interaction make restraint individually sensible, or does the one-time gain from cheating overwhelm the future punishment?
modeling_path: Start with the one-shot temptation. Then add the repeated relationship and compare today's deviation gain with the discounted stream of future losses. The model only supports cooperation when the future is heavy enough.
mathematical_spine: The spine is a discounted payoff comparison plus incentive compatibility. The intended cooperative action must give at least as much total discounted payoff as cheating once future punishment is included.
worked_walkthrough: If cheating gives an extra 5 today but causes a future loss of 2 each period, the result depends on patience. A very impatient seller treats the future loss as small and cheats. A patient seller may prefer preserving the high-price path.
where_simple_story_breaks: The simple story says repeated contact creates cooperation. The model says repetition only helps when monitoring, punishment, and patience make the no-cheating constraint pass.
what_to_check_in_transcript: Look for the repeated-game lectures connecting finite endings, infinite horizons, folk-theorem logic, and cartel applications. The evidence should show future punishment as a mechanism rather than a slogan.
why_this_case_matters: This case matters because it shows how time becomes an incentive device. The key idea is not that firms become friendly. The key idea is that today's shortcut can destroy a valuable tomorrow. Once future consequences are folded back into the present comparison, behavior that looked foolish in a one-shot game can become individually sensible under the right monitoring and punishment structure.
transfer_lesson: When transferring the lesson, turn any relationship claim into two payoff streams. One stream is stay on the cooperative path. The other is cheat now, collect the short-run gain, then live with the response. Compare those streams at the moment of temptation. Then check whether rivals can detect cheating and whether carrying out punishment later is itself rational, affordable, and legally possible.
failure_audit: The transfer can fail when the end of the relationship is known, buyers cannot observe price cuts, demand shocks hide cheating, punishments hurt the punishers too much, or laws change the available punishment. In those settings repetition is not enough. The model needs a monitoring story and a credible continuation story before a cartel or cooperation claim deserves the repeated-game label. It also needs a reason the same firms expect to meet again, not just a vague claim that the industry is ongoing.

title: Warranty Signal: when an action reveals hidden type only if imitation is costly
real_world_setup: A used-car seller can offer a warranty. Reliable sellers expect few repairs, while unreliable sellers expect many repairs. Buyers see the warranty but not the car's true quality.
first_principles_question: Does the warranty reveal quality, or would every seller imitate the same signal if buyers rewarded it?
modeling_path: Start by naming the hidden types. Then ask what each type would pay to send the signal and how buyers should update after seeing it. A signal separates types only when the cost and payoff differences make imitation unattractive for the wrong type.
mathematical_spine: The spine is belief updating plus incentive compatibility. Buyers use observed behavior to update beliefs, while the seller's action must be optimal for the type assigned to it in the proposed equilibrium.
worked_walkthrough: If a reliable seller expects warranty costs of 1 and an unreliable seller expects costs of 8, a price premium of 4 can make the warranty attractive to reliable sellers but unattractive to unreliable sellers. Then the action can carry information.
where_simple_story_breaks: The simple story says a warranty means quality. The model asks why a low-quality seller would not mimic that signal, and the answer must come from payoffs, not trust.
what_to_check_in_transcript: Look for Bayesian games, type spaces, perfect Bayesian equilibrium, and signaling. The evidence should support both belief movement and the incentive constraint that keeps messages meaningful.
why_this_case_matters: This case matters because it teaches the difference between evidence and decoration. A visible action becomes evidence only when different hidden types face different costs or benefits from taking it. Without that difference, the action may still persuade in a story, but it does not discipline beliefs in the model. The buyer's belief and the seller's incentive have to be solved together.
transfer_lesson: When transferring the lesson, ask what hidden type the action is supposed to reveal and why the wrong type would not copy it. The answer should be a payoff comparison, not a moral claim about honesty. Then ask how the receiver updates after observing the action and whether the receiver's response makes the sender's proposed action worthwhile for the intended type.
failure_audit: The transfer can fail if imitation is cheap, warranties are hard to enforce, buyers do not understand the signal, low-quality sellers can exit before repairs arrive, or the same signal is bundled with advertising. In those cases the signal may pool types rather than separate them. A careful paper should identify the separating cost, the receiver's belief update, and the sender's incentive constraint.

title: Ad Auction Design: when rules turn private values into bids and rankings
real_world_setup: A search platform sells ad slots. Advertisers differ in value per click and ad quality. The platform chooses a rule for ranking ads and charging winners.
first_principles_question: What behavior does the rule make individually sensible, and does that behavior produce the allocation the platform wants?
modeling_path: Start with bidders' private values and the allocation rule. Separate the chance of winning, the payment if winning, and the value created by clicks. Then ask whether the rule rewards truthful or strategically shaded behavior.
mathematical_spine: The spine is expected payment and incentive compatibility. A bidder compares value from winning against expected payment, while the platform designs the ranking and price rule that shapes those comparisons.
worked_walkthrough: If raising a bid increases the probability of winning from 20 percent to 70 percent while also raising payment if the ad wins, the bidder must compare both effects. In ad auctions, quality scores add another channel because better ads can change rank and expected value.
where_simple_story_breaks: The simple story says the highest bid wins. The course logic shows that auction format, payment rule, quality weighting, and beliefs about rivals all change the strategic incentives.
what_to_check_in_transcript: Look for the auctions, revenue equivalence, and ad-auction lectures. The evidence should support the separation between allocation, payment, bid shading, and rule design.
why_this_case_matters: This case matters because it shows that a market rule is a machine for shaping behavior. The platform is not just collecting bids; it is choosing what bidders must compare when they decide how to bid. A small change in ranking, pricing, reserve rules, or quality scoring can change the private calculation, which can change both revenue and which ads users actually see.
transfer_lesson: When transferring the lesson, split the mechanism into allocation and payment before using auction vocabulary. Ask who gets shown, what they pay, what private value they have, what information they hold, and what deviation is tempting. Then ask whether truth telling, bid shading, or quality improvement is the bidder's sensible response. The useful question is not what the auction is called, but what incentives its rule creates.
failure_audit: The transfer can fail if bidders have budgets, values are correlated, clicks are uncertain, quality scores are manipulable, participation repeats, or the platform has objectives beyond revenue. Revenue equivalence and textbook auction comparisons are fragile under those changes. A serious ad-auction argument should name which textbook assumptions survive and which part of the incentive calculation has been rebuilt for the platform setting. It should also separate advertiser welfare, user experience, and platform revenue instead of hiding them inside one ranking score.

title: Public Announcement: when the same fact changes behavior by becoming shared
real_world_setup: Many traders privately hear that a policy change is coming. Before the public announcement, each trader is unsure whether others heard the same information. After the announcement, everyone knows everyone heard it.
first_principles_question: Why can a public announcement matter if it does not add a new fact to some traders' private information?
modeling_path: Start by distinguishing truth from shared awareness. Private knowledge may not support coordination because each player is unsure about others' knowledge. A public event changes the levels of reasoning about what others know.
mathematical_spine: The spine is knowledge recursion. The model moves from the event itself, to everyone knowing the event, to everyone knowing everyone knows, and so on.
worked_walkthrough: If each trader privately heard the rumor, selling early may still feel risky because others may not act. A public announcement can make coordinated selling more likely because the fact becomes a shared anchor for expectations.
where_simple_story_breaks: The simple story says information is information. The model says publicness changes strategic meaning because action depends on beliefs about other people's beliefs.
what_to_check_in_transcript: Look for common knowledge and communication evidence. The evidence should distinguish private belief, public announcement, cheap talk, and equilibrium coordination.
why_this_case_matters: This case matters because it separates knowing a fact from being able to rely on other people knowing it. Strategic action often depends on shared confidence, not private awareness. A public announcement can change behavior even for people who already knew the content because it changes what they can infer about everyone else's knowledge and about everyone else's inference. The mechanism is not more raw information; it is a change in what each person can safely assume about the crowd.
transfer_lesson: When transferring the lesson, ask whether the action needs only private information or needs confidence about other people's information. If coordination is needed, identify the level of shared awareness the model requires. Then check the communication channel: was the message public, simultaneous, credible, and interpreted the same way? If the result depends on common knowledge, private leaks are not enough.
failure_audit: The transfer can fail if the announcement is not actually public, if different groups interpret it differently, if some players doubt who received it, or if sender incentives make the message cheap talk rather than reliable information. The case also changes when only a few layers of belief are needed. A careful paper should say why full common knowledge, rather than ordinary private belief, is the right object. It should also separate a public signal from a credible signal, because publicity alone does not make a self-interested sender truthful.
